assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks combine the magic-wavelength idea with ultracold strontium and ytterbium to reach 10^-18 fractional uncertainty. This is a step change in how precisely we can measure time, with clear consequences for relativistic geodesy, tests of fundamental constants and a future redefinition of the second. It is the kind of measurement advance that opens new ways to observe nature, which I weigh heavily.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and made the first demonstrations; Ye's group drove the record accuracy and stability and the link to frequency combs and Sr clocks. A two-person prize is clean. Other groups (for example NIST/JILA collaborators, PTB, SYRTE) contributed, but the decisive contributions are well localized, as far as I know. The frequency-comb part was already recognized in 2005.
assessment.maturity: Many independent labs reproduce clocks at the 10^-18 level, and comparisons between clocks are routine. The field is mature, and recognition would be timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee sees this as sufficiently distinct from the earlier ion-trap clock and frequency-comb prizes.
Exact credit split with Katori and Ye's collaborators, which I have not verified independently.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turned matter-wave coherence into a precision instrument: gravimeters, gradiometers, measurements of G and of the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. Real instruments exist and are used in the field. This matches my belief that progress is limited by how precisely we can measure.
assessment.attribution: Pritchard demonstrated early atom interferometers with material gratings and Na beams; Bordé developed the theory and the Ramsey-Bordé interferometer; Kasevich made the light-pulse gravimeters and gradiometers at precision scale. Schmiedmayer also pioneered atom-chip and BEC interferometry. Four credited names exceed three places, so Schmiedmayer's omission is a real allocation problem.
assessment.maturity: Commercial and field gravimeters exist and many groups reproduce the interferometers. Large-scale fundamental-physics tests are still developing, so the full payoff is partly in the future.
uncertainties: Which three of the four credited names are decisive.
Overlap with the 1997 and 2001 prizes on laser cooling and BEC.
Whether the fundamental-physics reach (e.g. equivalence principle, gravitational waves) has matured enough.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection and coherent control of single nitrogen-vacancy centres in diamond created a room-temperature solid-state qubit and a nanoscale sensor for magnetic fields, temperature and strain. It spans quantum information and applied measurement, including biological sensing. I know from my own work on crystals how hard it is to get long coherence in a solid, and NV centres show that it can be done.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko made the first single-NV optical detection and coherent spin control (1997 and early 2000s); Lukin's group developed quantum-sensing and register protocols and nanoscale NMR/magnetometry. Others (Awschalom, Hanson, Yacoby, Walsworth, Hollenberg) also made central contributions, so a three-person prize leaves out important people.
assessment.maturity: Strongly reproduced across many labs, with real instruments in use. Applications such as in-cell sensing are still developing.
uncertainties: Allocation versus Awschalom, Hanson and Yacoby, who are not credited here.
Distinguishing the discovery of single-NV detection from the later sensing and networking applications.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realize Hubbard models with tunable parameters, including the superfluid-Mott transition, single-site resolved quantum gas microscopes and fermionic Hubbard physics. It is a clean experimental platform that has changed how many-body physics is studied.
assessment.attribution: Greiner (with Hänsch and Bloch) observed the Mott transition; Bloch built the quantum gas microscope era and many experiments; Esslinger realized fermionic Mott and band insulators; Cirac and Zoller proposed the theory (Jaksch et al., Hubbard proposal). Five credited names against three places makes the allocation tough, and theory and experiment must be balanced.
assessment.maturity: The field is mature and widely reproduced, but quantum simulation's concrete results on open problems (e.g. the doped Hubbard model) are not yet fully settled.
uncertainties: Experiment versus theory credit split (Zoller and Cirac versus the experimentalists).
Whether the simulation has yet solved a problem inaccessible to classical methods.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Trapped-ion quantum computing, from the Cirac-Zoller gate proposal to experimental gates, entanglement of many ions and error-corrected operations, is a leading platform for quantum processors with the highest gate fidelities. It rests on very careful experimental work.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller made the 1995 proposal; Blatt's group demonstrated key gates, teleportation and large entangled states. Wineland and others (Monroe, Wineland's NIST group) already received the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems, and Wineland and Monroe are not credited here, which complicates the attribution.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced across many groups, and commercial machines are available. Whether trapped ions are the winning platform is still open, but the physics demonstrations are solid.
uncertainties: Whether proposal credit (Cirac, Zoller) is better paired with experimental credit (Blatt, Monroe), and Monroe is absent from the list.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED, with strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a microwave resonator, gave the dispersive readout and control architecture behind superconducting quantum processors. The measurements of coherence, readout fidelity and gate performance are concrete and impressive.
assessment.attribution: Blais, Girvin and Schoelkopf proposed and developed the theory; Wallraff and Schoelkopf demonstrated strong coupling (2004). Blais is credited as well, so four names compete for three places. The 2025 prize recognized macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits (Clarke, Devoret, Martinis), which is related, so a comparison is needed.
assessment.maturity: Very mature as a technology, widely reproduced and underpinning large industrial efforts. Timely, although the 2025 prize reduces the room for a close relative so soon.
uncertainties: Which of the four names to omit; theory versus experiment credit.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Ti:sapphire laser and passive mode-locking made femtosecond lasers practical and broadly available. This instrument enabled ultrafast spectroscopy, frequency combs and many other measurement techniques. Its impact on experimental physics, including my own field, is very large.
assessment.attribution: Moulton invented the Ti:sapphire gain medium; Sibbett's group discovered Kerr-lens mode locking; Keller developed semiconductor saturable absorber mirrors (SESAM). These are distinct contributions to the same instrument, and the split is a fair three-way prize, but the history of Kerr-lens contributions includes other names that I am not sure of.
assessment.maturity: Mature and in universal use since the early 1990s. Recognition might be seen as late but it is still defensible.
uncertainties: Close adjacency to the 2018 chirped pulse amplification prize and the 2023 attosecond prize.
Disputed priority within the Kerr-lens work.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Realization of strongly interacting Fermi gases and the BEC-BCS crossover gave a tunable, well-characterized system to study fermionic superfluidity, with Feshbach resonances, molecular BEC, vortices and thermodynamic measurements. It is a clean quantitative experiment-theory interface.
assessment.attribution: Grimm, Salomon and Thomas (with Jin, Ketterle, Zwierlein) all made key observations, such as molecular BEC, superfluidity and universal thermodynamics. Deborah Jin died in 2016, which makes the allocation harder, and Ketterle and Zwierlein are not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by multiple groups and well understood. The field is mature, though the discovery may feel diffuse.
uncertainties: Missing credits (Jin, Ketterle, Zwierlein) and the death of Jin.
